clue.text: Fixed bridal-car din in the name of a cocky red flier

indicators.note: fixed in the sense of rigged or doctored, so the letters of the phrase are rearranged

explanation.surface: Wedding-car hooting is put right, all in the name of a showy red bird.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fixed' is the anagram signal for the letters of 'bridal-car din'. 'cocky' means male, as in a cock bird: the male of this North American songbird is bright red.
explanation.definitionFit: The bright scarlet male of this American finch is the cock bird that flies about in red plumage.

clue.text: Smacking of army tips?

definitions.meaning: read as arm-y tips: the ends of the sleeves at the wrists, the cuff on each arm

explanation.surface: A soldier is slapped about while on duty at the front.
explanation.walkthrough: 'army' is not soldiers here but 'of the arm': the bands at the ends of shirt sleeves.
explanation.definitionFit: A smack round the head is a clout; the sleeve-ends at the wrist are the shirt's bands, so both readings use the same word.

clue.text: Disparage one in poor health

definitions.meaning: describes someone tired and unwell, a phrasal adjective for weak condition

explanation.surface: Belittling somebody who is already ill.
explanation.definitionFit: To criticise is to belittle someone; a tired, sickly person is said to be worn out in that same phrase.

clue.text: Pub taking in a sea signal officer when a quarter passes naturally

indicators.note: the pub takes the other pieces inside itself, so they go between its letters

parts.note: an inn is a pub
taken as written
SO is the abbreviation for signal officer

explanation.surface: A naval signaller drops into a seaside pub as the year turns.
explanation.walkthrough: A season is a quarter of the year; the phrase describes something happening at its natural time of year.
explanation.definitionFit: A season is one quarter of the year, so the phrase means at the time when that quarter comes round.

clue.text: An authorised check on one's account

definitions.text: An authorised check on one's account

parts.words: An authorised check on one's account
parts.note: an official inspection of the books, which are the account a firm keeps of its money

explanation.surface: A permitted cheque drawn on somebody's bank account.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a cheque drawn on a bank account; the sense is an official examination of financial records.
explanation.definitionFit: An official examination of a business's financial books is an authorised check of its accounts.

clue.text: Spirited counter broken against bottomless mountain

indicators.note: the counter word is broken up, so its letters are rearranged

parts.note: a bar is a counter in a pub
V, short for versus, means against

indicators.note: the mountain loses its last letter, its bottom in a down entry

parts.note: the Ural mountains of Russia

explanation.surface: A lively bar is smashed up near a mountain with its foot cut away.
explanation.walkthrough: 'broken' turns BAR into BRA; 'bottomless' cuts the L from URAL to leave URA.
explanation.definitionFit: A brilliant, daring performance shows great spirit, and the word also serves as an adjective for such dash.

clue.text: An alias of Lawrence taking in one composer?

parts.note: T. E. Lawrence enlisted in the RAF under the name Ross
taken as written
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: Lawrence of Arabia's pseudonym takes on a musician's identity.
explanation.walkthrough: T. E. Lawrence (of Arabia) served in the RAF as Aircraftman Ross; 'taking' just joins him to IN and I.
explanation.definitionFit: The Italian who wrote The Barber of Seville is one example of an opera writer, hence the question mark.

clue.text: Unwavering judgment needed where I find crime so uncontrolled

indicators.note: the letters run wild out of control, so they are rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone resolves to be tough when crime is out of control.
explanation.walkthrough: 'uncontrolled' is the anagram signal for the letters of 'I find crime so'.
explanation.definitionFit: A resolute, settled verdict is a judgment that does not waver.

clue.text: Minor article on Spanish princess

parts.note: a minor in law is an infant, someone under age
A is the indefinite article

explanation.surface: A small item about a young royal from Spain.
explanation.walkthrough: In law a minor is an infant; 'on' places the article after it.
explanation.definitionFit: In the Spanish royal family a daughter of the monarch who is not heir bears this title.

clue.text: An expensive address for a knight?

parts.note: dear means costly
a knight is addressed as Sir

explanation.surface: A pricey way of speaking to a knight.
explanation.walkthrough: 'address' is a form of words for opening a letter, not a home.
explanation.definitionFit: A formal letter opens with this salutation, a form of greeting to the reader.

clue.text: Fireworks in a passage of Caesar?

definitions.text: Fireworks in a passage of Caesar?

parts.words: Fireworks in a passage of Caesar?
parts.note: lights an ancient Roman might carry to show the way, read as the name of a kind of firework

explanation.surface: Pyrotechnics in a section of Caesar's writings.
explanation.walkthrough: A passage of Caesar suggests text, but read it as the lights an Italian of Caesar's time might carry; these are tube fireworks shooting coloured balls.
explanation.definitionFit: These are firework tubes that shoot out balls of coloured fire, named as if they were lights from ancient Rome.

clue.text: It was tender in Portugal's golden age

definitions.text: It was tender in Portugal's golden age

parts.words: It was tender in Portugal's golden age
parts.note: legal tender: a gold coin once current in Portugal, the age of gold coinage

explanation.surface: Something was gentle and loving in Portugal's heyday.
explanation.walkthrough: 'tender' is not gentle but legal tender, money; the coin was minted in gold in Portugal and circulated in Britain in the 18th century.
explanation.definitionFit: This was a Portuguese gold coin, legal currency in its day.

clue.text: An industry whose every package is designed for a break

definitions.text: An industry whose every package is designed for a break

parts.words: An industry whose every package is designed for a break
parts.note: the trade in holidays, where a package holiday is a break away from home

explanation.surface: A firm whose parcels are all made to be smashed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'package' and 'break' suggest fragile parcels, but they mean package holidays and short breaks.
explanation.definitionFit: The holiday trade sells package deals made for travellers taking a break.

clue.text: Nigel's become marbles champion

indicators.note: Nigel has become something else, so his letters are rearranged

parts.note: the 's stands for has and adds no letter

explanation.surface: Nigel has turned into a winner at the game of marbles.
explanation.walkthrough: The Elgin Marbles are the Parthenon sculptures that Lord Elgin brought to Britain; he is their champion, not a winner at the children's game.
explanation.definitionFit: Lord Elgin removed the Parthenon sculptures to Britain, and they still bear his name, so he is their advocate.

clue.text: Tout is in a peculiar position

indicators.note: odd or strange, so the letters are put in an odd order

explanation.surface: A ticket tout finds himself in an odd spot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'peculiar' is the anagram signal for the letters of 'Tout is in a'.
explanation.definitionFit: A location or set of circumstances is a place or post, so the two words are synonyms.

clue.text: Treasury violated; Esau's hurt

indicators.note: the letters are violated or desecrated, so their order is broken

parts.note: the 's here is a letter of the fodder
taken as written

explanation.surface: Esau feels wronged after his birthright treasure was plundered.
explanation.walkthrough: 'violated' is the anagram signal for the letters of 'Esau's hurt'; a treasury is a store of riches, here of words.
explanation.definitionFit: A collection of words grouped by meaning is called a treasury of words, the Greek source meaning a storehouse.

clue.text: In no sense could a state of guilt be pronounced

definitions.text: In no sense could a state of guilt be pronounced

indicators.note: said out loud, the words give a single word that sounds the same

parts.note: spoken quickly, these three words run together into one word

explanation.surface: Under no circumstances could anyone declare a state of guilt.
explanation.walkthrough: Said aloud, 'In no sense' gives the word for being guiltless, and the whole clue describes that: a state in which guilt could never be declared.
explanation.definitionFit: Being free of any guilt means no verdict of guilty could ever be given.

clue.text: It seems there isn't any syllabus worth recording

parts.note: no means none at all
a table is a schedule or timetable, as a syllabus sets out what is taught

explanation.surface: Apparently the course has no plan worth writing down.
explanation.walkthrough: 'It seems' is a link phrase; a table here is a timetable or schedule.
explanation.definitionFit: Something remarkable deserves to be noted down, so it is worth recording.

clue.text: Drink to Bach's fifty-one variations

indicators.note: a musical variation reworks a theme, so these letters are rearranged

parts.note: the 's here is a letter of the fodder
LI is fifty-one in Roman numerals

explanation.surface: A toast to the composer Bach's set of fifty-one musical variations.
explanation.walkthrough: 'variations' is the anagram signal for BACHS plus LI, the Roman numeral for fifty-one.
explanation.definitionFit: This dry white Burgundy wine is a drink.

clue.text: It might make a spaghetti junction of Pennsylvania station

definitions.text: It might make a spaghetti junction

parts.note: PA is the postal abbreviation for Pennsylvania

explanation.surface: A tangle of roads by a station in Pennsylvania.
explanation.walkthrough: Spaghetti Junction is the nickname of a famous tangled motorway interchange near Birmingham, England; here it is read literally as a meeting of spaghetti.
explanation.definitionFit: Spaghetti is an example of this Italian food, so a heap of it could form a junction of strands.

clue.text: One policeman confining cool characters for making high-blown noise

indicators.note: the policeman holds the other piece inside him

parts.note: PC is short for police constable
I is the Roman numeral for one

indicators.note: the letters of cool are taken as characters to rearrange

explanation.surface: A constable locks up a calm person amid shrill whistling.
explanation.walkthrough: 'One policeman' reads as one officer, but it is I and PC separately; 'characters' tells you to treat 'cool' as letters to rearrange, and 'high-blown' points to a shrill wind instrument.
explanation.definitionFit: This small flute sounds an octave above the ordinary one, giving a high-pitched blown sound.

clue.text: Bear put us in a spot

indicators.note: us is placed inside the spot word

parts.note: a stain is a spot or mark
taken as written

explanation.surface: A bear lands us in trouble.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bear' looks like the animal, but it is the verb meaning to support or endure.
explanation.definitionFit: To bear a weight is to hold it up, to support or endure it.

clue.text: Where the efficient commuter hopes to get things organised?

definitions.text: Where the efficient commuter hopes to get things organised?

parts.words: Where the efficient commuter hopes to get things organised?
parts.note: the place a rail commuter sits, aboard the carriage, read also as a phrase meaning in proper order

explanation.surface: A tidy-minded commuter sorts out work on the journey.
explanation.walkthrough: The phrase means both aboard a railway carriage and in order, under way.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase means in progress or in order, and literally aboard a railway carriage.

clue.text: Drainwork couldn't be lower

indicators.note: the letters are worked, as in worked over, so they are rearranged

explanation.surface: Work on the drains is as low as a job can get.
explanation.walkthrough: 'work' is the anagram signal for the letters of 'Drain'.
explanation.definitionFit: The lowest point of something cannot go further down.

clue.text: Accountant accustomed to being charged

parts.note: used to something means accustomed to it

explanation.surface: An accountant has grown used to paying fees.
explanation.walkthrough: 'being charged' suggests a fee, but it means accused of a crime.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone formally charged with a crime stands indicted.

clue.text: Writer's tip: Slovene lake produced many little bites

parts.note: a nib is the point of a pen
Bled is a lake in Slovenia

explanation.surface: A travel writer's advice: a Slovenian lake teems with midge bites.
explanation.walkthrough: 'tip' suggests advice, but it is the point of a pen; Lake Bled is a well-known resort in Slovenia.
explanation.definitionFit: To take lots of small bites is to gnaw at something gently.

clue.text: It might be apple producers' underground system

definitions.text: It might be apple producers' underground system

parts.words: It might be apple producers' underground system
parts.note: the network below ground of an apple tree, the producer of apples

explanation.surface: Apple growers run a secret underground network.
explanation.walkthrough: 'apple producers' are apple trees, and their underground system is the mass of roots.
explanation.definitionFit: The root system of a plant is its anchorage below the soil.

clue.text: A sweet scoop from Sheffield, perhaps

definitions.text: A sweet scoop from Sheffield, perhaps

parts.words: A sweet scoop from Sheffield, perhaps
parts.note: a piece of cutlery for pudding, Sheffield in England being famous for steel cutlery

explanation.surface: An ice-cream scoop bought in Sheffield.
explanation.walkthrough: Sheffield, an English city, is famous for its steel cutlery; a sweet is a pudding, and the scoop is the spoon used for it.
explanation.definitionFit: This mid-sized spoon is used for eating puddings.
